endings.text: Night on the 14th. The bundle is tied, the calico folded under the blankets, the keg stoppered beside the pot. You did both errands and kept the household's water clean of the fort's grog. Wau-Bun says that in the morning the band played the Dead March as the troops left the fort, and that Wells had blackened his face 'in token of his impending fate.' What happened on the beach is told in the jaunt The Battle of Fort Dearborn.

Night on the 14th. You carried home the news from the gate, and tonight the story of the medal, which nobody in the settlement can stop repeating. Nobody can unpack now. Wau-Bun says that in the morning the band played the Dead March as the troops left the fort. Tomorrow at nine the column walks south along the beach. What happened there is told in the jaunt The Battle of Fort Dearborn.

Night on the 14th. The calico from the factory is folded on top of the bundle, and you watched the last evening at the fort. You know now how much was given away, on whose orders, and that the man who gave the order blamed the man who obeyed it. Tomorrow at nine the gate opens. What happened on the beach is told in the jaunt The Battle of Fort Dearborn.

Night on the 14th. The keg is full, the bundle is tied, and you know who rode in at the gate and which way the column walks in the morning. Nobody in the house sleeps much. Tomorrow at nine the gate opens and the column walks south. What happened on the beach is told in the jaunt The Battle of Fort Dearborn.

evidence.locator: Quaife Appendix III (Heald's journal) and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text
evidence.text: Heald's journal: 'On the 9th of Augt, 1812, rec'd orders from Genl Wm. Hull to evacuate the Post of Chicago and proceed with my Command to Detroit.' Quaife: 'The next day the Indian runner. Winnemac, delivered to Captain Heald at Fort Dearborn his order for the evacuation.' Wau-Bun puts the runner, Winnemeg or Catfish, a Potawatomi, at the post on the 7th, bringing despatches that 'announced the declaration of war between the United States and Great Britain'. Wau-Bun: 'The order for evacuating the post was read next morning upon parade', and the officers' 'unanimous advice was, to remain where they were, and fortify themselves as strongly as possible.' Quaife defends Heald: 'Obedience to orders is the primary duty of a soldier.'

evidence.locator: Wau-Bun, the April section; the Reader, the sutler paragraph; Kirkland, the Helm narrative
evidence.text: Wau-Bun (1856): 'On the north side of the main stream, but quite near its junction with Lake Michigan, stood (as has already been described) the dwelling-house and trading-establishment of Mr. Kinzie.' 'The fort was situated on the southern bank, directly opposite this mansion'. The Chicago Reader (2018): in January 1812 Heald made 'Messrs. Kinzie & Forsyth' the exclusive fort sutlers. Kirkland (1893): Margaret Helm was the 'step-daughter of old John Kinzie'.

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 15th, at 9 o'clock in the morning, we commenced our march: a part of the Miamies were detached in front, and the remainder in our rear, as guards, under the direction of Captain Wells. The situation of the country rendered it necessary for us to take the beach, with the lake on our left, and a high sand bank on our right, at about 100 yards distance.' Wau-Bun: 'As the troops left the fort, the band struck up the Dead March', and Wells 'had blackened his face before leaving the garrison, in token of his impending fate.' Mrs. Kinzie's boat 'had scarcely reached the mouth of the river, which, it will be recollected, was here half a mile below the fort, when another messenger from To-pee-nee-bee arrived to detain them where they were.' Quaife lists the order: Wells and part of the Miamis, the garrison, the women and children, the twelve Chicago militia.

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The surplus arms and ammunition I thought proper to destroy, fearing they would make bad use of it if put in their possession. I also destroyed all the liquor on hand after they began to collect.' Wau-Bun: 'The same evening the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well which had been dug there to supply the garrison with water in case of emergency; the remainder was transported as secretly as possible through the northern gate, the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river.' The muskets 'were broken up and thrown into the well'. The noise betrayed it, and 'the taste of the water the next morning was, as one expressed it, "strong grog."'

evidence.text: Wau-Bun: on the evening after the second council 'Black Partridge, a conspicuous chief, entered the quarters of the commanding officer' and gave back his medal: 'I will not wear a token of peace while I am compelled to act as an enemy.' Quaife: Black Partridge was 'a Pottawatomie chief from the Illinois River' (a Potawatomi leader); of the two contemporary versions, Lieutenant Helm's and Sergeant Griffith's through McAfee, both record his warning and 'Helm alone mentions the surrender of the medal.'

evidence.reasoning: Wau-Bun's 'evening succeeding the council' and the march next morning; the hour is a reading of 'evening'.
evidence.text: Wells reached the fort on the 13th by Heald's report or the 14th by Wau-Bun; Black Partridge came to the commanding officer 'on the evening' after the second council. This stop is set at sunset on 14 August, the eve of the march.

evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, footnote 413, 'Index annexed to the draught of Fort Dearborn &c.', Whistler, 20 February 1808 (Gutenberg #69274 plain text), Whistler's note
evidence.text: Whistler, 20 February 1808, closing his note to the draught: 'At this time the Garrison (except the Houses on the Opisite side of the river being somewhat in the way) is perfectly secure from any ambuscade or Barrier.' His index numbers the 'Wharf of said River' and 'John Kinzie Esq. House on the opisite side River'. He had already had a picket fence across the river taken up, since it 'might serve as a Barrier against the Garrison', and 'replaced with a common rail fence.'

evidence.reasoning: Wau-Bun dates the goods to the 13th and the well 'The same evening'; Heald's report dates the goods to the 14th and Wells to the 13th, and Wau-Bun has Wells on the 14th. The medal came on the evening after the second council, read as the 14th as The Battle of Fort Dearborn reads it. The hours are chosen to walk the two days in order, not recorded.
evidence.text: The walk runs over the last two days before the march of 15 August 1812: the 13th, when Wau-Bun has the factory goods given out and, that evening, the ammunition and liquor sunk, and Heald's report has Wells come in; and the 14th, the evening Black Partridge gave back his medal. The hours of the stops are the jaunt's pacing; no source gives them.

evidence.reasoning: The anchors and their positions are the ones The Battle of Fort Dearborn and Fort Dearborn, Building by Building stand on, read from Whistler's 1808 draught, Quaife's description of the fort and Wau-Bun's placing of the Kinzie house opposite it. This jaunt adds no place.
evidence.text: The six stops are scene anchors of 1812 that the published 1812 jaunts already use: the front of the Kinzie house on the north bank, the factory front, the main gate, the covered way at the north-east corner, the parade and the river mouth. No interior is entered and no doorway is claimed.

The young person the visitor plays, their age, their household outside the pickets and its packing, the errands, the order of the route, the two choices, the four endings, the timing inputs and the A Bundle for the March keepsake are invented connective narrative. No such young person is recorded or named, no named person is met or speaks to them, no known child of a named family is given a part, and nothing is staged at any stop.

opening.text:
JAUNT: PACKING FOR THE MARCH. August 1812, and you are twelve. Your household lives in a log house outside the pickets of Fort Dearborn, on the south bank of the Chicago River, among the few families who live off the garrison and its trade. The United States is at war with Britain. The general at Detroit has ordered the post given up, and blamed its want of provisions on the man who commands it. In two days the garrison marches out, and your household marches with it, because there is nowhere else to go.

The places and the records are real; the young person is you. You will not meet the captain or the chief, and nobody explains anything to a child. Watch, carry, and choose your errands, knowing less than the grown people around you, who know less than they would like.

premise: Play a young person of the settlement in the last two days before the garrison leaves Fort Dearborn, 13 and 14 August 1812: choose your errands, and pack for the march.

choices.consequence: You will see what the garrison gives away.
choices.label: To the factory, where the goods are going out

choices.consequence: You will hear who is coming in before anyone tells you.
choices.label: To the gate, to listen for news

stops.narrative: Which errand first: the factory, or the gate?
stops.text: Thursday, 13 August 1812, morning, on the north bank, outside 'the dwelling-house and trading-establishment of Mr. Kinzie', whose firm holds the sole right to sell to the fort. On the 9th, Heald wrote, the order came to 'evacuate the Post of Chicago and proceed with my Command to Detroit.' It was read on parade, and the officers' 'unanimous advice was, to remain where they were, and fortify themselves as strongly as possible.' Captain Heald will obey; a later historian defends him with 'Obedience to orders is the primary duty of a soldier.' At nine on the 15th the garrison marches, and with it the women and children and the twelve men of the town's militia. Everything your household owns must be sorted: carried, given away, or left behind. Your mother has two errands for you across the river.

stops.narrative: What the garrison cannot carry, it gives away.
stops.text: Afternoon at the factory, the government's trading house, a log house just south-west of the fort. The shelves are emptying: 'blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints'. Heald's report says he gave out 'all the goods in the factory store, and a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us.' Hull's order, written 'with regret', blamed the evacuation on 'the want of Provisions only a neglect of the Commandant'. The same order let the goods go to 'the Friendly Indians' who might escort the garrison to Fort Wayne. It also named 'the Poor & needy of your Post', and your household is poor enough to be counted. Next door the agent's house has its piazzas 'planked up, for greater security', with port-holes cut. You carry home a bolt of calico, and nothing else.

stops.narrative: News comes in at the gate before it reaches anyone's house.
stops.text: Afternoon at the main gate, in the middle of the south side. The fort is a square of two-storey barracks with blockhouses at opposite corners, 'inclosed within a double row of palisades'. Riders come in: Captain William Wells of Fort Wayne, by Heald's report 'with about 30 Miamies, for the purpose of escorting us in, by the request of General Hull.' Wau-Bun has him a day later, come to save 'his relative, Captain Heald', and 'all too late': the ammunition was already gone. Rebekah Heald, the captain's wife, is his niece. Nobody at the gate explains any of this to you, but you can read the faces of the men who hear it. You listen, and carry the news home with the water bucket.

choices.consequence: Your household will have clean water for the walk.
choices.label: Fill the keg upstream tonight

choices.consequence: You will see who comes and goes on the last day.
choices.label: Stay near the fort tomorrow

stops.narrative: Draw water upstream tonight, or wait until morning?
stops.text: Evening, on the river side of the fort's north-east corner, where a covered way runs down to the water. Tonight the soldiers work in it. 'The same evening the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well'. The muskets 'were broken up and thrown into the well'. The rest of the liquor goes out of the northern gate, 'the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river.' Heald gave his reason: 'fearing they would make bad use of it if put in their possession.' The fort is sinking its powder and pouring out its drink in the dark. It is meant to be secret, but the knocking carries, and next morning the water tastes of 'strong grog'. Your household's water comes from this river.

stops.narrative: The last full day, spent packing.
stops.text: Friday, 14 August, morning, where the river meets the lake, half a mile below the fort. In 1808 Captain Whistler drew 'John Kinzie Esq. House on the opisite side River' and called the garrison 'perfectly secure from any ambuscade or Barrier', apart from the houses across the river being 'somewhat in the way'. Wau-Bun says Mrs. Kinzie's boat will come down to this river mouth tomorrow while the column walks. Your household goes on foot. Your keg is full and stoppered, and today you sort the rest: a blanket each, the pot, the calico or the news, and what stays behind for strangers. Tomorrow the column takes the beach south, 'with the lake on our left, and a high sand bank on our right'.

stops.narrative: A warning on the last evening.
stops.text: Friday, 14 August, evening, on the parade inside the fort, beside the commanding officer's quarters on its east side. Black Partridge, 'a Pottawatomie chief from the Illinois River', has come in. Wau-Bun says he 'entered the quarters of the commanding officer' and gave back his peace medal: 'I will not wear a token of peace while I am compelled to act as an enemy.' Lieutenant Helm and Sergeant Griffith both recorded his warning; 'Helm alone mentions the surrender of the medal.' You see no more than a door closing across the parade. Afterwards you hear the grown people repeat his words, and hear them fail to agree on what the captain should do now. Tomorrow at nine the gate opens anyway.

title: Packing for the March
